name: Ukwuani / Úkwúánì
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 5 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Okumo, Franca & Chibunma Amara Bright-Ajoku. 2020. Syllable and tonal structures of Úkwúánì noun. Journal of Languages, Linguistics and Literary Studies (JOLLS) 9(5): 1-9. Open access (CC BY-NC-ND), AJOL 311133,https://www.ajol.info/index.php/jolls/article/view/311133
catalog_locator: p.1 (sec. 1 Introduction, right column); p.2 (sec. 2.1 end, Okumo 2017 summary; sec. 2.2 = the only occurrence of 'stress', a generic SPE remark); p.4 (sec. 4.1 opening); p.8-9 (Conclusion, tone restrictions)
catalog_quote: Ukwuani is a tone language in that variation in pitch of segmentally or grammatically identical pairs can bring about a change in meaning. It has three contrastive tones which include two register tones: high [H] marked with an acute accent [´] and low [L] marked with a grave accent [`] and a falling contour [HL] marked with [^]. ... According to Okumo (2017), Ukwuani is a tone language with two register tones and one contrastive contour tone. ... Based on the number of syllables and the inherent tonal patterns, Úkwúánì nouns can be classified into four major groups ... From the analysis, we observed some restrictions on tones in Úkwúánì: The monosyllabic nouns have a basic high tone and are very few in number. The falling contour cannot occur at the initial position. It occurs after a high or low tone as earlier illustrated in the disyllabic and trisyllabic nouns. For disyllabic nouns, a final L is very rare except for some personal names.
world_status: statement found in an open source

The falling contour cannot occur at the initial p…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Ukwuani is described purely as a lexical tone language (H, L, falling HL; tone borne by vowels and syllabic nasals), with noun tone melodies LL/LH/LF/HH/HL/HF etc. and positional restrictions on the falling tone; the primary describer gives no word-stress or accent rule. A secondary student study (Ochonogor 2025, Table 3 p.130) adds explicitly 'Stress: Not contrastive' for Ukwuani/Igbo.
new_statements.exceptions: Tonal restrictions only: falling contour never word-initial; disyllabic nouns rarely end in L except personal names; monosyllabic nouns inherently H.
new_statements.domain_note: Statements concern lexical tone on citation-form nouns (SIL Africa Area wordlist data); no phrase-level or stress domain discussed.
new_statements.identity_note: All opened sources describe Ukwuani proper (Ndokwa/Ukwuani LGAs, Delta State), the 'Ukwuani' member of Glottolog's Ukwuani-Aboh-Ndoni (ukwu1241, ISO ukw); nothing found for the Aboh or Ndoni varieties. Ochonogor 2025 treats Ukwuani as a dialect of Igbo and pools it with Igbo speakers, so its figures are not cleanly Ukwuani.

tone_statements.citation: Bright-Ajoku, Chibunma Amara & Franca Okumo. 2020. A comparative analysis of tone in the Igbo and Ukwuani. Journal of Language and Linguistics (JOLL) 6(3) (June 2020): 89-105. ISSN 2659-0689. Awka: Nnamdi Azikiwe University. (no DOI; OJS article 118)
tone_statements.quote: We found out that both Igbo and Ukwuani employ the use of tones for lexical and grammatical functions. While Igbo has two level distinctive tones comprising a high and low tone and a grammatical downstep, Ukwuani has three distinctive tones consisting of a high, low and falling contour. [...] Whereas for Ukwuani, a three way contrast occurs after a low tone as: Low-Low, Low-High and Low-Falling. After a high tone, a two way distribution occurs: High-High and High-Falling.
tone_statements.locator: abstract, p. 89; inventory statement repeated in section 4.1, p. 92 and conclusion p. 103

tone_statements.quote: The two language also has similar tonal pattern which are high, low and a tonal phenomenon known as down step. They both operate two level tones thereby making them a typical example of register tone language and their tonological processes are also similar.

sources.quote: p. 7: "The tones are shown in the system which they developed, viz.: low is always marked with a grave accent, `, high is left un-marked, and the high-tone syllable immediately after downstep (so-called 'mid') is marked with a macron, ¯. ... In my view, Igbo is most economically analyzed as having two tones, high and low. Between high tones we often have a downstep, as a juncture feature or juncture phoneme." p. 11: "There is one other very striking unifying factor which is obvious from these lists. This is the extraordinary stability of tone through the whole range of the dialects studied." p. 13: "5. Ukwaali. The list represents the speech of Mr. Anthony Chigonti, of Umu Kwaata, about fifty miles from Sapele, along the Asaba road. Collected by R. G. Armstrong in 1965 and 1966." pp. 21-22: "Since Ukwaali is still little known, it may be useful to give some of the pronoun sets as additional data. Disjunctive pronouns: (all tones marked)" followed by the pronoun, 'I killed a goat', 'I did not kill a goat', 'my farm', 'my father', 'my mother' paradigms carrying grave (low) and macron (post-downstep high) marks, e.g. the 'goat' word written with macrons (nee-wu) after the verb.

tone.quote: Adopting a descriptive-morphological approach, the study identifies seven main processes: affixation, reduplication, compounding, and tone-based derivation. Findings show that Úkwúání relies heavily on prefixal and tonal changes for nominalization and verb derivation, uses reduplication for intensification and plurality, and forms compounds with a head-modifier order.

tone.quote: To begin with, Ụkwụanị is a tone language which does not use stress. Consequently, the concepts of stressed syllables and ‘unstressessed syllables’ are not known by the typical and linguistically naive Ụkwụanị speakers of English as L2. Consequently, they cannot manage stress.
